approachQuestion.prompt:
Loan devices

A nondecreasing array need lists the minimum capacity required by each request. A second nondecreasing array size lists available device capacities. Assign at most one device to a request and at most one request to a device; a device works when its capacity is at least the request’s requirement. Return the maximum number of requests served. Requests have no other preferences or priorities.

Example 1: need=[2,3,5], size=[1,3,5] → 2.
Example 2: need=[1,1,1], size=[1,2] → 2.
Example 3: need=[], size=[5] → 0.

Constraints: 0 ≤ r=len(need), d=len(size); n=r+d ≤ 200000; capacities and requirements are integers from 1 to 10^9. Both arrays are already nondecreasing, with duplicates allowed. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Use one index into each sorted array. Discard devices smaller than the smallest unserved requirement. Otherwise match the current device to that requirement, increment the count, and advance both indices. Stop when either array ends.
options.feedback: A too-small device cannot serve this or any later request. For a sufficient device, using the smallest sufficient one on the least demanding request preserves larger devices. Any optimum can exchange its assignments to contain this match without reducing its count.

options.text: Match each device to the most demanding request it can serve, discarding any request it cannot currently serve.
options.feedback: Discarding a hard request before seeing a later larger device loses opportunities. For need=[1,3] and size=[1,3], discarding request 3 at device 1 leaves only one match instead of two.

options.text: Use the smallest request and largest device at each step, then remove both after every successful match.
options.feedback: A large device may be needed by a harder request. For need=[1,3] and size=[1,3], pairing 1 with 3 leaves the 3 request unserved; the optimum serves both.

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method. Let r and d be the two array lengths and n=r+d. Both arrays are already sorted. Use two scalar indices and a count; do not copy the arrays, allocate match records or recurse. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: Each device is considered once and each satisfied request advances once.

messages.text: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
The scans do not restart for each item.
In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.

details: Each iteration consumes a device and may also consume a request, and neither index moves backward. Worst-case work is O(r+d)=O(n), with O(1) scalar auxiliary state. Arrays and returned count are excluded. There is no sorting, copying, hashing or recursion.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
